x.ASV: A Psalm of Asaph. Surely God is good to Israel, Even to such as are pure in heart.
x.Darby: A Psalm of Asaph. TrulyGod is good to Israel, to such as are of a pure heart.
x.KJV: A Psalm of Asaph. Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.
x.YLT: A Psalm of Asaph. Only--good to Israel is God, to the clean of heart. And I--as a little thing, My feet have been turned aside,

nt: The psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize the truth of what follows. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation or use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]
Here, **Israel** represents the Israelite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the people of Israel]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of righteous people as **pure** and not blemished by wrong and sinful thoughts in contrast to having a **heart** that is impure because of sinful thoughts and motives and therefore morally dirty. What the psalmist means by **pure** here is that the person’s **heart** is “morally pure.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [to the ones who think about and want what is pleasing to God] or [to those with a morally pure heart]

In Jewish culture people considered the **heart** to be the center of a persons thoughts and feelings and here, the **heart** represents the intentions, thoughts and desires of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to those who think about and want what is pure] or [to those with a pure mind] or [to those with pure thoughts]

x.ASV: But as for me, my feet were almost gone; My steps had well nigh slipped.
x.Darby: But as for me, my feet were almost gone, my steps had well nigh slipped;
x.KJV: But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.

nt: כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י

Here, **my feet** and **my steps** represent the Psalmist himself and the phrases **slipped** and **slide out** refer to abandoning doing what pleases God and instead choosing to sin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with an equivalent expression or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was tempted to stop obeying God. It was as if my feet almost slipped and as if my steps were almost caused to slide out from under me] or [I almost stopped trusting in God; I was almost guilty of sinning against him]
כִּ֭⁠מְעַט נטוי רַגְלָ֑⁠י כְּ֝⁠אַ֗יִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָֽ⁠י

The phrases **my feet almost slipped** and **my steps almost were caused to slide out from under me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [my feet almost slipped] or [my feet almost slid out from under me]

The expression **my steps almost were caused to slide out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the following verse implies that the Psalmist caused his own steps to almost slide out from under him when he looked at the “prosperity of the wicked” and did not also immediately go into “God’s sanctuary” so that he could “understand” the final “fate” of the wicked (see [Psalm 73:17](../073/017.md)). Alternate translation: [I almost caused my steps to slide out from under me]

x.ASV: For I was envious at the arrogant, When I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
x.Darby: For I was envious at the arrogant, seeing the prosperity of the wicked.
x.KJV: For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

nt: Here the word **because** indicates that what follows it in this verse is the reason for what precedes it in [73:2](../073/002.md). Use a natural form for indicating this relationship. Alternate translation: [for]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [when I saw the prosperity of the wicked, I was envious of the arrogant]

The Psalmist is using the adjectives **arrogant** and **wicked** as nouns in order to describe certain people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate these words with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [of arrogant people when I saw the prosperity of wicked people] or [of the people who are arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the people who are wicked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prosperity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I saw how prosperous the wicked were]

x.Darby: For they have no pangs in their death, and their body is well nourished;
x.KJV: For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm.

nt: The word the ULT translates as **ropes** refers to ropes or bonds that constrain a person. Alternate translation: [struggles] or [emotional pains] or [pains]

The word the ULT translates as **until their death** could refer to: (1) the time before the death of wicked people in which case you can use the ULT as a model, or (2) the time at which wicked people die. Alternate translation: [in their death] or [at their death]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people, and with people they are not afflicted] or [other people, and they are not afflicted like everyone else]

The expression **they are not afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that God did it. Alternate translation: [and God does not afflict them like he does the rest of man] or [and God does not afflict them like he does everyone else]

x.ASV: Therefore pride is as a chain about their neck; Violence covereth them as a garment.
x.Darby: Therefore pride encompasseth them as a neck-chain, violence covereth them [as] a garment;
x.KJV: Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them as a garment.

nt: Here, the word **Therefore** introduces the result of [73:4–5](../073/004.md). You can use a natural word or phrase in your language to express this relationship. Alternate translation: [As a result]

The psalmist is speaking of **pride** as if it were a **necklace** that wicked people wear around their neck. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparison, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they wear pride like a necklace] or [pride is like a necklace which they flaunt]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they act pridefully for all to see, like someone who wears a necklace that they want everyone to see] or [they unashamedly act proud in front of everyone, like a person wearing a necklace that they want everyone to see]

A **necklace** is a type of jewelry worn around the neck in order to adorn the body and make a person look more attractive. If your readers would not be familiar with necklaces, you could use the name of something similar that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternately, if you are using footnotes, you could make a footnote explaining what a **necklace** is. Alternate translation: [a neck ornament for them]

The psalmist is speaking of **violence** as it were a **garment** that people wear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning with a comparable expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [violence covers them like a garment] or [violence covers them like clothing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are proud of their violent actions and display them openly, as a person who wears a garment for all to see]

Here the psalmist speaks of the **heart** of a wicked person as if it were a container that could overflow with evil **imaginations** (thoughts). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express the meaning using an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their heart is constantly thinking of evil things to do] or [their heart is constantly imagining evil thoughts]

The psalmist is describing the mind of wicked people by association with their **heart**, which is where a person’s thoughts and intentions were viewed as coming from in Jewish culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they constantly think of evil things to do] or [the imaginations of their inner being overflow]

x.KJV: They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **evil** and **oppression**, you could express the same ideas in some other way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and wickedly speak about oppressing people]

The phrase **they speak from an elevated place** means “they speak arrogantly.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly. Alternate translation: [they speak arrogantly]

x.ASV: They have set their mouth in the heavens, And their tongue walketh through the earth.
x.Darby: They set their mouth in the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.
x.KJV: They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.

nt: Here, **mouth** and **tongue** represents “speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They talk as if they are God who is in the heavens, and their speech goes through the earth]

The word translated as **in the heavens** could be translated as: (1) **in the heavens** as modeled by the ULT in which case the psalmist is describing the role or authority of God by association with the **heavens**, Alternate translation: [They talk with their mouth as if they are God who is in heaven] or [They talk as if they are in the position of God] or (2) “against the heavens” in which case the psalmist is describing God by association with the **heavens**. The expression **are drained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must state who did the action, the context implies that people did it. Alternate translation: [and they drain the waters of a full cup]

x.ASV: And they say, How doth God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?

nt: The phrases **How does God know** and **is there knowledge in the Most High** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases into one. Alternate translation: [How could God know?] or [Does God have knowledge?]

Here the word **they** could refer to: (1) wicked people. Alternate translation: [And those who are wicked say] or [And the wicked say] or (2) people who are righteous and obey God. Alternate translation: [And righteous people say] or [And godly people say]

Here wicked people are not asking for information but are using the question form to express that they do not think God knows or cares about the evil things they do. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Surely God does not know what we are doing! Surely the Most High has no knowledge of it!] or [Surely God does not care about we are doing! Surely what we are doing does not matter to the Most High!]
This portion of this verse is a quotation of what the wicked people said or thought to themselves. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

x.ASV: Surely in vain have I cleansed my heart, And washed my hands in innocency;
x.Darby: Truly have I purified my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency:
x.KJV: Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.
x.YLT: Only--a vain thing! I have purified my heart, And I wash in innocency my hands,

nt: Here the psalmist uses the word **Surely** to emphasize his strong thoughts and feelings about the certainty of what he states in this verse. Use a natural form in your language for expressing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [Certainly]

The psalmist is describing his thoughts and intentions by association with his **heart**, which Jews viewed as the center of a person’s thoughts and intentions. The expression **I have kept my heart clean** means he has intentionally kept his thoughts and intentions morally pure (free from sin). You may have an equivalent expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have kept my thoughts pure]

The psalmist is describing his actions by association with his **hands**, which he would use to do the actions. The psalmist is using the symbolic action of hand washing to declare his **innocence**. In that culture hand washing was a common practice that people did to publicly assert that they were innocent. (See Deuteronomy [21:6](../../deu/21/06.md) and Matthew [27:24](../../mat/27/24.md).) Here the psalmist is saying that he has **washed** his **hands in innocence** as a way to declare that he is guiltless. See how you translated the similar phrase in [Psalm 26:6](../026/006.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and kept my actions pure to show that I am innocent] or [and kept my actions free from sin]
